Graph Traversal via Connected Mobile Agents

Saswata Jana ††thanks: Supported by Prime Minister’s Research Fellowship (PMRF) scheme of the Govt. of India (PMRF-ID: 1902165) Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Guwahati, India    Giuseppe F. Italiano Affiliation: Luiss University, Rome, Italy    Partha Sarathi Mandal E-mail  Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Guwahati, India
Abstract

This paper considers the Hamiltonian walk problem in the multi-agent coordination framework, referred to as kk-agents Hamiltonian walk problem (kk-HWP). In this problem, a set of kk connected agents collectively compute a spanning walk of a given undirected graph in the minimum steps. At each step, the agents are at kk distinct vertices and the induced subgraph made by the occupied vertices remains connected. In the next consecutive steps, each agent may remain stationary or move to one of its neighbours. To the best of our knowledge, this problem has not been previously explored in the context of multi-agent systems with connectivity. As a generalization of the well-known Hamiltonian walk problem (when k=1k=1), kk-HWP is NP-hard. We propose a (3−121)(3-\frac{1}{21})-approximation algorithm for 2-HWP on arbitrary graphs. For the tree, we define a restricted version of the problem and present an optimal algorithm for arbitrary values of kk. Finally, we formalize the problem for kk-uniform hypergraphs and present a 2​(1+ln⁡k)2(1+\ln k)-approximation algorithm. This result is also adapted to design an approximation algorithm for kk-HWP on general graphs when k=O⁡(1)k=O(1).

Keywords: 
Approximation Algorithms; Graph Traversal; Mobile Agent;
Hamiltonian Walk; Hypergraphs.

1 Introduction

Graph traversal is a fundamental problem in computer science and robotics, where the goal is to visit every node of a graph at least once. A key objective of graph traversal is to minimize the number of steps needed to traverse the entire graph. Typically, such tasks can be accomplished by a single agent. However, relying on a single agent can be inefficient, prone to failure, and unsuitable for large or complex environments. These limitations motivate the need for multi-agent systems, where the agents coordinate among themselves to traverse the whole graph while reducing the traversal time and handling failures effectively. One major challenge in coordinating multiple agents is ensuring safe and reliable communication during the traversal. In many practical systems, such as swarm robotics or drone networks, connectivity among agents is essential to maintain real-time coordination, prevent collisions, and quickly react to unexpected failures. In addition, the connectivity constraint also plays a key role in fault-tolerant settings. For instance, if one agent fails, the connected agents can detect the failure and either compensate for the loss or design a strategy to recover the lost functionality.

Preliminaries, Related works and Problem definition: Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a simple undirected connected graph (without self-loops and multiple edges), where VV is the set of vertices and EE is the set of edges. An edge between two vertices viv_{i} and vjv_{j} is denoted by (vi,vj)(v_{i},v_{j}). Let n=|V|n=|V| be the number of vertices and m=|E|m=|E| be the number of edges of GG. N⁡(v)N(v) is the open neighbourhood of the vertex v∈Vv\in V, consisting of all its neighbours, while N⁡[v]N[v] is the closed neighbourhood of vv, defined as N⁡[v]=N⁡(v)∪{v}N[v]=N(v)\cup\{v\}. A sequence of distinct vertices P={v1,v2,⋯,vp}P=\{v_{1},v_{2},\cdots,v_{p}\} is called a path of the graph GG if (vi,vi+1)∈E​∀i∈{1,2,⋯,p−1}(v_{i},v_{i+1})\in E~\forall i\in\{1,2,\cdots,p-1\}. Whenever both endpoints of a path v1v_{1} and vpv_{p} are explicitly mentioned, we denote the path as Pv1​vpP_{v_{1}v_{p}}. Additionally, if v1=vpv_{1}=v_{p}, the sequence is called a cycle of the graph GG. If GG admits a path of length (n−1)(n-1), then the path is called a Hamiltonian path. Similarly, if a graph has a cycle of length nn, then the cycle is called a Hamiltonian cycle, and the graph is called Hamiltonian graph. In other words, a graph is called Hamiltonian if there exists a cycle that passes through each vertex of GG exactly once. The problem of finding a Hamiltonian cycle in a graph, or checking whether a given graph is Hamiltonian, is known as the Hamiltonian cycle problem, which is one of Karp’s 21 NP-complete problems [13]. Given that a class of graphs lacks a Hamiltonian path or cycle, there is growing interest in determining a minimum-length spanning walk of those graphs. A walk is a path with some possible repeated vertices. If both endpoints of the walk are the same (or different), the walk is termed a closed (or open) walk. A walk is a spanning walk of GG if it passes through each vertex of GG at least once. A closed spanning walk of minimum length is termed as Hamiltonian walk. The length of a Hamiltonian walk of the graph GG is known as Hamiltonian number and denoted as h+​(G)h^{+}(G). If h+​(G)=nh^{+}(G)=n, the graph GG is Hamiltonian and vice versa. n≤h+​(G)≤2​(n−1)n\leq h^{+}(G)\leq 2(n-1). It is well known that h+​(G)=2​n−2h^{+}(G)=2n-2 iff GG is a tree [9]. An open spanning walk of GG is a spanning walk with different endpoints, and we use the notation h−​(G)h^{-}(G) to denote the length of the minimum open spanning walk of GG. Finding the minimum-length open spanning walk of a graph is known as the open Hamiltonian walk problem. If the graph GG is Hamiltonian, then h−​(G)=(n−1)h^{-}(G)=(n-1). However, the converse is not true.

The challenge of finding an open spanning walk is closely related to the classic traveling salesman problem (TSP), in which the objective is to locate a minimum weight Hamiltonian cycle in a given complete weighted graph. Christofides-Serdyukov [5] [16] proposed a 32\frac{3}{2}-approximation algorithm for TSP if the weight function satisfies the triangular inequality. After decades, Karlin et al. [12] give a randomized 32−ϵ\frac{3}{2}-\epsilon approximation algorithm for some ϵ>10−36\epsilon>10^{-36}. A polynomial time approximation scheme (PTAS) exists for some special instances of the TSP, such as for Euclidean TSP [2], [15], planar TSP [1], [10], [14], and bounded genus TSP [6]. The multiple traveling salesman problem [4] is a generalization of the TSP, where multiple salesmen independently (no restriction to the connectivity) visit the vertices of the graph. Hoogeveen [11] modified Christofide’s heuristic to find a minimum weight Hamiltonian path of a given weighted complete graph when the weights satisfy the triangular inequality. The modified heuristic also gives a 32\frac{3}{2} approximation factor, which is still the best-known factor for the problem. We can apply the modified Christofides heuristic to find an open spanning walk for an undirected, unweighted, and connected graph GG by converting it into a complete weighted graph. To do this, we assign a weight equal to one to each existing edge and add all missing edges with a weight equal to the length of the shortest paths between corresponding vertices.

We address the open Hamiltonian walk problem from the perspective of a mobile agent that explores the entire graph GG in a minimum number of steps, starting from an arbitrary vertex. At each step, the agent can move to one of its neighbouring vertices. Therefore, any minimum open-spanning walk constitutes a feasible solution. Additionally, we can apply the modified Christofide’s heuristic [11] to obtain a 32\frac{3}{2}-approximation algorithm for the problem. In this paper, we formulate the generalized version of the Hamiltonian walk problem, which we named as kk-agent Hamiltonian Walk problem (k-HWP), where a set of k(≥1)k~(\geq 1) agents collectively explore the graph. The constraint is that at any instant of time t(≥0)t(\geq 0), kk agents must lie on kk distinct vertices of GG, so that the subgraph induced by the vertices occupied by the kk agents must be connected. Initially, the agents can start from any arbitrary vertices that satisfy the above constraints. In the next step, all agents move synchronously to one of their neighbouring vertices or choose to remain stationary. Let A={a1,a2,⋯,ak}A=\{a_{1},a_{2},\cdots,a_{k}\} be the set of kk agents. We use vitv_{i}^{t} to denote the vertex viv_{i} occupied by a agent aia_{i} at the tt-th step. We denote the configuration at the tt-th step by 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}, and defined by the kk-tuple (v1t,v2t,⋯,vkt)(v_{1}^{t},v_{2}^{t},\cdots,v_{k}^{t}), where vit≠vjt,∀i≠jv_{i}^{t}\neq v_{j}^{t},\forall i\neq j and the subgraph induced by the set of vertices {v1t,v2t,⋯,vkt}⊆V\{v_{1}^{t},v_{2}^{t},\cdots,v_{k}^{t}\}\subseteq V is connected. For convenience, we slightly abuse the notation 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} to denote the set {v1t,v2t,⋯,vkt}\{v_{1}^{t},v_{2}^{t},\cdots,v_{k}^{t}\} and, more generally, any arbitrary configuration. Two configurations, 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} and 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}, are said to be adjacent if ∀i∈{1,2,⋯,k}\forall i\in\{1,2,\cdots,k\} either vit=vit′v_{i}^{t}=v_{i}^{t^{\prime}} or (vit,vit′)∈E(v_{i}^{t},v_{i}^{t^{\prime}})\in E. We imagine a graph whose vertices correspond to configurations, where two vertices are adjacent if the corresponding configurations are adjacent. We refer to the edge between two adjacent vertices, i.e., configurations, as a transition edge. The objective of kk-HWP is to find a sequence of configurations {𝒞0,𝒞1,⋯,𝒞l}\{\mathcal{C}_{0},\mathcal{C}_{1},\cdots,\mathcal{C}_{l}\} with a minimum length (i.e., ll is minimum) such that each vertex of GG appears in at least one configuration in the sequence, and there is a transition edge between every two consecutive configurations. In other words, the objective is to find an open spanning walk of configurations {𝒞t}t=0l\{\mathcal{C}_{t}\}^{l}_{t=0} of minimum length, where each vertex in this walk is a kk-tuple configuration and ∪t=0l∪i=1kvit=V\cup_{t=0}^{l}\cup_{i=1}^{k}v_{i}^{t}=V. We denote the length of this open walk by hk−​(G)h^{-}_{k}(G). If there are (l+1)(l+1) many configurations in the walk, then hk−​(G)=lh^{-}_{k}(G)=l. When k=1k=1, h1−​(G)h_{1}^{-}(G) coincides with h−​(G)h^{-}(G). An open walk of configurations is called a transition walk. Since we focus solely on the open walk in this paper, we use hk​(G)h_{k}(G), instead of hk−​(G)h^{-}_{k}(G), to denote the length of the minimum open spanning walk of configurations for the graph GG with kk agents. The NP-completeness of kk-HWP follows from the fact that when k=1k=1, it is equivalent to the Hamiltonian walk problem, which is known to be NP-complete. We present the formal definition of kk-HWP below.

Definition 1 (Problem: kk-HWP)

Consider an undirected connected graph GG and a collection of kk agents. The goal is to find a sequence of configurations of minimum length such that each successive pair in the sequence is adjacent, and every vertex in GG is included at least once in one of these configurations.

When k=2k=2, any configuration represents an edge of GG. Therefore, we can interpret the problem as traversing the graph through its edges.

Definition 2 (rr-transition edge)

The transition edge between two configurations 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} and 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} is said to be a rr-transition edge if 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} has exactly rr vertices that are not in 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}.

For example of a rr-transition edge, let k=4k=4, 𝒞t=(v1,v2,v3,v4)\mathcal{C}_{t}=(v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4}) and 𝒞t′=(v5,v2,v4,v6)\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}=(v_{5},v_{2},v_{4},v_{6}). If 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} and 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} are adjacent, then the edge between them is called a 22-transition edge. The transition edges of kk-HWP can be categorized into kk distinct classes based on the value of r∈{1,2,⋯,k}r\in\{1,2,\cdots,k\}. We disregard 00-transition edges, which indicate that agents either remain stationary or rearrange their positions without visiting new vertices. Since our objective is to identify a transition walk of minimum length, we consistently strive to minimize the number of configurations encountered during any transition walk. For example, let 𝒞t=(v1,v2,v3,v4)\mathcal{C}_{t}=(v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4}), 𝒞t′=(v2,v4,v3,v1)\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}=(v_{2},v_{4},v_{3},v_{1}) and 𝒞t′′=(v5,v6,v7,v8)\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime\prime}}=(v_{5},v_{6},v_{7},v_{8}). Suppose that a transition walk includes the configuration 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}, followed by 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}, and then 𝒞t′′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime\prime}}. The transition edge between 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} and 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} is 00-transition edge. We can modify the walk by removing 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} and replacing 𝒞t′′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime\prime}} with 𝒞t′′′=(v8,v5,v7,v6)\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime\prime\prime}}=(v_{8},v_{5},v_{7},v_{6}). The modification is valid because the configurations 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}, 𝒞t′′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime\prime}} are adjacent, implies (v1,v8),(v2,v5),(v3,v7),(v4,v6)(v_{1},v_{8}),(v_{2},v_{5}),(v_{3},v_{7}),(v_{4},v_{6}) all belonging to EE, implies 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}, 𝒞t′′′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime\prime\prime}} are adjacent. By making this change, we eliminate the 00-transition edge.

1.1 Our Contribution

In this paper, our contributions are the following:

  • •

    We define kk-agents Hamiltonian walk problem (kk-HWP).

  • •

    For the tree, we propose an optimal algorithm when k≤3k\leq 3. For any value of kk, we present an optimal algorithm for the restricted version of the problem on tree, where we only allow 1-transition edges (Theorem 2.3).

  • •

    We give a (3−121)(3-\frac{1}{21})-approximation algorithm on arbitrary graphs for k=2k=2 (Theorem 3.1).

  • •

    We extend the problem definition to hypergraphs and propose a 2​(1+ln⁡k)2(1+\ln k)-approximation algorithm for kk-uniform hypergraphs (Theorem 4.1). This algorithm is further developed into an approximation algorithm for kk-HWP, when k=O⁡(1)k=O(1) (Theorem 4.2).

2 Algorithms for Tree

Since the kk-HWP problem is NP-hard for general graphs, our goal is to explore specific graph classes where optimal solutions can be achieved. This section examines kk-HWP problem on acyclic graphs and presents results for a constrained version of the problem. First, we describe an optimal strategy (1-HWP-For-Tree) to solve 1-HWP for tree. This serves as a foundation for understanding the generalized strategy (for arbitrary values of kk), which we discuss later in the section. A vertex is called leaf (or pendant) if it has degree one. The diameter of the graph GG, denoted d​i​a​m​(G)diam(G), is the length of the longest path.

Description of the Algorithm (1-HWP-For-Tree): Let P∗=Pv1∗​v2∗P^{*}=P_{v_{1}^{*}v_{2}^{*}} be a longest path of the tree GG. Then, both v1∗v_{1}^{*} and v2∗v_{2}^{*} must be leaves of GG. The agent starts the traversal from v1∗v_{1}^{*} and aims to eventually reach v2∗v_{2}^{*} while traversing all the vertices. If multiple unexplored vertices are available, it prioritizes those not located on P∗P^{*}. Whenever all adjacent vertices are explored, it backtracks to its parent vertex. A parent vertex of vv is the vertex from which the vertex vv is explored for the first time. The pseudocode of the Algorithm is provided in Algorithm 1. We analyze the algorithm below.

Lemma 1

The walk returned by 1-HWP-For-Tree is a spanning walk of GG with length 2​(n−1)−d​i​a​m​(G)2(n-1)-diam(G), where d​i​a​m​(G)diam(G) is the diameter and nn is the number of vertices of GG.

Proof

Steps (6 - 14) from the pseudocode of Algorithm 1 justify that the agent lying on an explored vertex vv backtracks (move to the parent) only when it finds all its neighbouring vertices explored. However, an agent lying on P∗P^{*} never backtracks, as it always finds an unexlored neighbour lying on P∗P^{*}. So, the existence of unexplored vertex (∉P∗)(\notin P^{*}) means that the agent backtracks despite having an unexplored neighbour, which is a contradiction. Additionally, all the vertices on P∗P^{*} must be explored as there is a unique way to reach v2∗v_{2}^{*} from v1∗v_{1}^{*}, which is through P∗P^{*}.

Let (x,y)(x,y) be an arbitrary edge in EE. Without loss of generality, we assume that xx is the parent of yy. If (x,y)∈P∗(x,y)\in P^{*}, the agent never moves back to xx from yy, as it must encounter an unexplored neighbour vertex z∈P∗∩N⁡(y)z\in P^{*}\cap N(y) and moves to it (steps 10-11). If (x,y)∉P∗(x,y)\notin P^{*}, then yy also does not lie in P∗P^{*}. Here, when the agent reaches yy, it returns to x⁡(p​a​r​e​n​t​(y))x(parent(y)) after confirming that every vertex in N⁡(y)N(y) has been explored (steps 13-14). Consequently, all the edges that do not belong to P∗P^{*} are traversed twice in the walk produced by the algorithm. Therefore, the length of the walk is 2​(n−1)−d​i​a​m​(G)2(n-1)-diam(G), as the tree has (n−1)(n-1) edges and the number of edges in the longest path equals the diameter of the tree. ∎

Remark 1

Algorithm 1 runs polynomially. This is because we can find the diameter of the graph in linear time ( in terms of nn). All other operations per transition also take polynomial time, since all checks and assign operations for a vertex are done in at most |N⁡(v)|≤Δ|N(v)|\leq\Delta time, where Δ\Delta is the maximum degree of the tree GG. So the algorithm needs in total O⁡(n)+∑O⁡(Δ)O(n)+\sum O(\Delta) time, where the summation is over number of steps required by the algorithm, which is at most 2​n2n. Hence the overall time complexity of the algorithm is O⁡(n⋅Δ)O(n\cdot\Delta) time.

Lemma 2

For a tree GG with nn vertices, h1​(G)≥2​(n−1)−d​i​a​m​(G)h_{1}(G)\geq 2(n-1)-diam(G).

Proof

Any open spanning walk must contain each edge of the tree at least once. Consider an optimal spanning walk WW, which starts from the vertex viv_{i} and ends at vjv_{j}. Since the graph is a tree, there is always a unique path PP between viv_{i} and vjv_{j}. Let (x,y)∈E(x,y)\in E be an edge that does not belong to PP. We will prove that (x,y)(x,y) must appear twice in this walk. Then WW is the union of either (i) the sub-walk viv_{i} to xx with no internal yy, then xx to yy, and finally the sub-walk yy to vjv_{j}, or (ii) the sub-walk viv_{i} to yy with no internal xx, then yy to xx, and then the sub-walk xx to vjv_{j}. For the first case, the edge (x,y)(x,y) is encountered for the first time when it traverses from xx to yy. Then again when traverses from yy to vjv_{j}, as there is an unique path between yy and vjv_{j} which contains xx. Similarly, we can prove for the second case. However, any edge lying on PP may not meet either of the above two conditions. So, the length of the walk WW is l​e​n​(W)=h1​(G)≥len(W)=h_{1}(G)\geq (total number of edges) + (number of edges not in PP) ≥(n−1)+(n−1−d​i​a​m​(G))\geq(n-1)+(n-1-diam(G)), since the length of PP is at most d​i​a​m​(G)diam(G). ∎

Hence we have an algorithm (1-HWP-For-Tree) for 1-HWP on tree, which returned a spanning walk that matches with the lower bound of h1​(G)h_{1}(G). Therefore, combining Lemma 1, 2 and Remark 1, we can state the following theorem.

Theorem 2.1

Algorithm 1-HWP-For-Tree provides an optimal solution for 1-HWP in polynomial time, when the input graph GG is a tree.

Using the above strategy, we now design an algorithm for a restricted version of kk-HWP on trees, where the restriction is on the type of transition edges allowed between two configurations. We begin with the following structural property.

Theorem 2.2

If GG is a tree and the edge between two configurations 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} and 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} in the kk-HWP is an rr-transition edge, then r≤⌊k2⌋r\leq\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor, where k≥2k\geq 2.

Proof

We first prove that there must exist a vertex vv in 𝒞t∩𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t}\cap\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}. Suppose, on the contrary, that 𝒞t∩𝒞t′=∅\mathcal{C}_{t}\cap\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}=\emptyset. In such a scenario, there exist two distinct paths between the vertices vitv_{i}^{t} and vjtv_{j}^{t}, where vitv_{i}^{t} and vjtv_{j}^{t} are the positions of the agents aia_{i} and aja_{j}, respectively, in the configuration 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}. Since the induced graph G⁡[𝒞t]G[\mathcal{C}_{t}] made by the vertices of 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} is connected, there exists a path between vitv_{i}^{t} and vjtv_{j}^{t} that entirely lies in G⁡[𝒞t]G[\mathcal{C}_{t}]. An alternative path proceeds via the edge (vit,vit′)(v_{i}^{t},v_{i}^{t^{\prime}}), followed by a path within G⁡[𝒞t′]G[\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}] from vit′v_{i}^{t^{\prime}} to vjt′v_{j}^{t^{\prime}}, and concludes with the edge (vjt′,vjt)(v_{j}^{t^{\prime}},v_{j}^{t}). The existence of two such distinct paths contradicts the fact that there is always a unique path between two vertices in a tree.

Now consider a vertex vit′∈𝒞t′∖𝒞tv_{i}^{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{t}. We claim that vit∈𝒞t′v_{i}^{t}\in\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}. Otherwise, there would exist two paths between some v∈𝒞t∩𝒞t′v\in\mathcal{C}_{t}\cap\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} and vit′v_{i}^{t^{\prime}}: one passing through vitv_{i}^{t} and the other does not, which is again a contradiction. Hence, for every vit′∈𝒞t′∖𝒞tv_{i}^{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{t}, the corresponding vit∈𝒞t∩𝒞t′v_{i}^{t}\in\mathcal{C}_{t}\cap\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}. In other words, for each new vertex of the current configuration (𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}), we always have a unique vertex that is part of both the current and previous configuration (𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}). Thus the proof. ∎

The above result implies that when k≤3k\leq 3, all transition edges are necessarily 11-transition edges. For larger values of kk, between the movements of one configuration to the other, the agents might encounter k/2k/2 new vertices. To simplify the transition structure and enable the design of an optimal algorithm, we consider a restricted version of kk-HWP, where each transition edge must be a 11-transition edge, regardless of the number of agents (k)(k). We refer to this problem as kk-agents restricted Hamiltonian walk problem (kk-RHWP). We present a polynomial-time algorithm, kk-RHWP-For-Tree, that computes an optimal solution to the kk-RHWP on trees. The optimal length of the kk-RHWP on GG is denoted by hkr​(G)h^{r}_{k}(G). Note that h2r​(G)=h2​(G)h^{r}_{2}(G)=h_{2}(G) and h3r​(G)=h3​(G)h^{r}_{3}(G)=h_{3}(G). We introduce subsequent definitions (Definition 3, 4 ), which are limited to the tree.

Definition 3 (Problem: kk-RHWP)

Consider an undirected connected graph GG along with a collection of kk agents. The objective is to find a sequence of configurations of minimum length such that between every two consecutive configurations in the sequence there is a 1-transition edge, and every vertex of GG is included at least once in one of these configurations.

Definition 4 (Explored edge or vertex)

Let 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} and 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} be two adjacent configurations in a transition walk of kk-RHWP; then there exists exactly one vertex vit′∈𝒞t′∖𝒞tv_{i}^{t^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{t}. We say that the edge (vit,vit′)(v_{i}^{t},v_{i}^{t^{\prime}}) is explored (or encountered) by the transition from 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} to 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} or the vertex vit′v_{i}^{t^{\prime}} is explored (or encountered).

Next, we describe the algorithm kk-RHWP-For-Tree for solving kk-RHWP on trees. We designate one of the agents as the head, who explores the graph. All other agents either follow the head or remain stationary to maintain connectivity.

Description of the Algorithm (kk-RHWP-For-Tree): Let P∗=Pv1∗​v2∗P^{*}=P_{v_{1}^{*}v_{2}^{*}} be a longest path of GG. All vertices are initially unexplored. Agents are initially deployed using the strategy 1-HWP-For-Tree. The agent aia_{i} is placed at the vertex vi0v_{i}^{0}, the ii-th explored vertex by 1-HWP-For-Tree. So, the initial configuration 𝒞0\mathcal{C}_{0} equals (v10,v20,⋯,vk0)(v_{1}^{0},v_{2}^{0},\cdots,v_{k}^{0}), where v10=v1∗v_{1}^{0}=v_{1}^{*}. We refer to the vertices vk0v_{k}^{0} and v10v_{1}^{0} as the head (vH)(v_{H}) and the tail (vT)(v_{T}) of the current configuration, respectively. Additionally, we apply the terms head and tail to agents at vHv_{H} and vTv_{T}, respectively. The head takes priority in exploring the graph. If the head encounters a situation where it finds all its neighbours as explored, it locates the nearest occupied vertex that has at least one unexplored neighbour. This vertex then becomes the new head, while the previous head is designated as the new tail. If the head has multiple unexplored neighbours, it selects the vertex vv, which does not lie on P∗P^{*}, as its next target of movement and sets p​a​r​e​n​t​(v)=vHparent(v)=v_{H}. If the neighbours of all the occupied vertices (including head) in the current configuration are explored, the agent aia_{i} closest to P∗P^{*} becomes the new head, while the previous head becomes the new tail. In this case, agent aia_{i} decides its target as p​a​r​e​n​t​(v′)parent(v^{\prime}), where v′v^{\prime} is the current position of aia_{i}. Once the head sets its target for the next movement, all the agents lying on the path between head and tail, including the tail, will move simultaneously in the direction of the head, while all other agents remain stationary. If the tail is not a leaf vertex of the induced graph G′G^{\prime}, which is formed by all occupied vertices, then moving the tail would disconnect G′G^{\prime}. In such a case, we assign the tail to one of the leaf vertices of G′G^{\prime}, excluding both the head and the vertex nearest to P∗P^{*}, if possible. Once all the agents between vHv_{H} and vTv_{T} have moved to their designated targets, we update the head and tail accordingly. Whenever the vertex v2∗v_{2}^{*} becomes the head, the algorithm terminates. The pseudocode is mentioned in Algorithm 2.

Lemma 3

The walk of configurations returned by the algorithm kk-RHWP-For-Tree is a spanning walk of GG of length tA​L​Gt_{ALG} = (n−k)+∑e∈EdP∗k​(e)(n-k)+\sum_{e\in E}d^{k}_{P^{*}}(e), where P∗P^{*} is the longest path of GG between the vertices v1∗v_{1}^{*} and v2∗v_{2}^{*} selected by the algorithm.

Proof

The initial deployment of the agents encountered exactly kk vertices, which is assured by the correctness of Algorithm 1-HWP-For-Tree. Similar to Algorithm 1-HWP-For-Tree, we only move backward to the parent vertex when all the neighbours of the kk-agents are explored, which confirms that each vertex must be in either the initial configuration or encountered by some subsequent configuration. To prove the second part of the lemma, it is sufficient to prove that any edge with dP∗k​(e)=0d^{k}_{P^{*}}(e)=0 encountered exactly once and an edge with dP∗k​(e)=1d^{k}_{P^{*}}(e)=1 encountered exactly twice. First, we will prove that any edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) lies on P∗P^{*} encountered exactly once, where vv is nearer to v2∗v_{2}^{*} than uu. Let vv be explored for the first time by the configuration 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}. Since an agent (head) lies at uu moves to v∈P∗v\in P^{*} only when all other neighbours of uu are already explored. As the final target is v2∗v_{2}^{*} and vv is nearer to v2∗v_{2}^{*} than uu, no agent being a head ever moves back to uu from vv. Therefore, the edge ee is encountered exactly once. Now, we will prove that any edge e=(u,v)∉P∗e=(u,v)\notin P^{*} can be encountered at most twice by the algorithm. The edge ee is encountered when we reach a configuration with the head as uu, and then it sets its next target for the movement as vv. After this, if the algorithm reaches a configuration with the head as vv and all the vertex in the configuration are explored, then at the next configuration, it encountered ee again by moving the agent lie at vv to uu, which is the p​a​r​e​n​t​(u)parent(u). Afterward, we can not have a configuration with an agent lying on uu as the head and vv as its next target, as vv has already been explored. So, the algorithm counters an edge at most twice. Next we show that, an edge ee, with dP∗k​(e)=0d^{k}_{P^{*}}(e)=0, encountered exactly once. We will discuss the extreme case. A similar argument will follow for the other case. Let us consider an edge e=(x,y)e=(x,y) such that the height of the sub-tree TP​(e)T_{P}(e) rooted at yy is exactly (k−2)(k-2). Let ee be first encountered by the configuration 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}. All the later configurations that encountered the other vertices of TP​(e)T_{P}(e) must contain the edge ee, as we never make the vertex xx (which is nearest to P∗P^{*} among all the occupied vertices) as the tail (vTv_{T}) of those configurations (Step 33-34). This shows that all the configurations contain the edge e⁡(x,y)e(x,y). In the next configuration vHv_{H} changes to xx and vTv_{T} changes to y3y_{3} and moves to the next configuration 𝒞t+6=(z,y2,y,x)\mathcal{C}_{t+6}=(z,y_{2},y,x) with vH=z,vT=y2v_{H}=z,v_{T}=y_{2}. Thus the lemma follows, i.e., the length of the walk is (n−1)−(k−1)−∑e∈P∗dP∗k​(e)(n-1)-(k-1)-\sum_{e\in P^{*}}d^{k}_{P^{*}}(e), (n−1)(n-1) referred as the number edges to be encountered, (k−1)(k-1) is subtracted as those many are covered in the initial configuration and the last part say that those edges are encountered twice. ∎

Lemma 4

The time needed for the Algorithm k-RHWP-For-Tree is O⁡(n⋅k⋅Δ)O(n\cdot k\cdot\Delta), where kk is the number of agents, nn is the number of vertices, and Δ\Delta is the maximum degree of the tree GG.

Proof

The diameter of a tree can be computed in O⁡(n)O(n) time using the depth-first search (DFS) twice, which is a very standard process. First, perform a DFS from an arbitrary node (considered the root) to identify the node that is furthest from it. Then, perform a second DFS starting from that furthest node. The maximum distance discovered in this second traversal is the diameter of the tree. From Remark 1, the initial deployment can also be completed in O⁡(n)O(n) time. Thereafter, at each step, we need to identify an occupied vertex that has at least one unoccupied neighbour. For each such vertex vv, we can check whether it has any unexplored neighbours—or determine that all its neighbours are already explored—in O⁡(Δ)O(\Delta) time, where Δ\Delta is the maximum degree of the graph. In the worst case, none of the occupied vertices have unexplored neighbours. In that case, we have to check for all the occupied vertices starting from the head, which requires O⁡(k​Δ)O(k\Delta) time, as there are kk many occupied vertices in each step (configuration). In addition, if the tail is not located at the the leaf of G′G^{\prime}, the induced subgraph made by the occupied vertices, then we have to transfer the tail. The construction of G′G^{\prime} and the execution of the transfer (if needed) again take O⁡(k)O(k) time. Therefore, each transition from one configuration to the next can be completed in at most O⁡(k​Δ)O(k\Delta) time. From Lemma 3, the algorithm terminates after at most (n−k)+∑e∈EdP∗k​(e)≤(n−k)+(n−d​i​a​m​(G))<2​n(n-k)+\sum_{e\in E}d^{k}_{P^{*}}(e)\leq(n-k)+(n-diam(G))<2n steps. The total time complexity of the algorithm is O⁡(n⋅k⋅Δ)O(n\cdot k\cdot\Delta). ∎

Let tO​p​tt_{Opt} be the length of an open spanning walk of configurations with kk agents, returned by an optimal algorithm O​p​tOpt. Then tO​p​t≥(n−k)+∑e∈EdPO​p​tk​(e).t_{Opt}\geq(n-k)+\sum_{e\in E}d^{k}_{P_{Opt}}(e).

Proof

Any initial configuration of kk-HWP covers exactly (k−1)(k-1) many edges of GG. Consider all the edges ee with dPO​p​tk​(e)=1d^{k}_{P_{Opt}}(e)=1. To prove the lemma, it is sufficient to prove that all such edges ee must be encountered at least twice by the algorithm O​p​tOpt. Let e=(u,v)e=(u,v), where uu is the vertex nearer to PO​p​tP_{Opt} than vv. By Definition 5, there must exist a leaf zz such that the distance between uu and zz is at least kk. Let the edge ee be encountered in some configuration (𝒞t)(\mathcal{C}_{t}) when an agent lies at uu and moves to vv. After 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}, the edge ee is again encountered, as the algorithm O​p​tOpt terminates after exploring the vertex yS​o​ly_{Sol}. Thus, it must cross the edge ee while moving to yS​o​ly_{Sol} after 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}.

For example, consider Fig. 3. Let PO​p​t=Px​yP_{Opt}=P_{xy} and k=3k=3. We have dPO​p​tk​(e)=1d^{k}_{P_{Opt}}(e)=1. Let, the edges ee and (u,v)(u,v) encountered for the first time by the configurations 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} and 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}, respectively. Then the inequality t′≥t+2t^{\prime}\geq t+2 must hold and 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}} consists of the vertices {v,w,z}\{v,w,z\}. The edge ee is encountered again after 𝒞t′\mathcal{C}_{t^{\prime}}, as the last encountered vertex is yy. ∎

For a tree GG, hkr​(G)≥(n−k)+∑e∈EdP∗k​(e)h_{k}^{r}(G)\geq(n-k)+\sum_{e\in E}d^{k}_{P^{*}}(e), where P∗P^{*} is the longest paths of the tree GG joining two vertices v1∗v_{1}^{*} and v2∗v_{2}^{*}, which is selected by the Algorithm k-RHWP-For-Tree.

The above analysis shows that the algorithm k-RHWP-For-Tree returns a spanning walk of GG whose length matches the lower bound of hkr​(G)h_{k}^{r}(G). Therefore, combining Lemmas 3, 4, 5, and 6, we establish the following theorem.

Theorem 2.3

Algorithm k-RHWP-For-Tree provides an optimal solution for k-RHWP in polynomial time, when the input graph GG is a tree.

3 Algorithms for Arbitrary Graph in Case of k=2

Here, we present an approximation algorithm for the 2-HWP on an arbitrary graph GG. We start by introducing a simple algorithm that achieves an asymptotic approximation factor of 3, using the relationship between h1​(G)h_{1}(G) and h2​(G)h_{2}(G).

h1​(G)≤2⋅h2​(G)+1.h_{1}(G)\leq 2\cdot h_{2}(G)+1.

The length of W1W_{1} is at most 2​p+12p+1. Therefore, h1​(G)≤2​p+1≤2​h2​(G)+1.h_{1}(G)\leq 2p+1\leq 2h_{2}(G)+1. ∎

The Approximation Algorithm for 2-HWP: Let W1={v1,v2,⋯,vl+1}W_{1}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\cdots,v_{l+1}\} be a spanning walk of configurations with one agent using some known β\beta-approximation algorithm for the open Hamiltonian walk problem. Then l≤β⋅h1​(G)l\leq\beta\cdot h_{1}(G). The walk W1W_{1} can be converted to a spanning walk of configurations W2W_{2} with two agents, where W2={(v1,v2),(v2,v3),⋯,(vl,vl+1)}W_{2}=\{(v_{1},v_{2}),(v_{2},v_{3}),\cdots,(v_{l},v_{l+1})\}. The length of the walk W2W_{2} is (l−1)≤β⋅h1​(G)−1≤2​β⋅h2​(G)+(β−1)(l-1)\leq\beta\cdot h_{1}(G)-1\leq 2\beta\cdot h_{2}(G)+(\beta-1), by Lemma 7. The best known approximation factor for the Hamiltonian walk problem is 3/23/2 by Hoogeveen [11]. Hence, we have a solution of size at most (3​h2​(G)+1)(3h_{2}(G)+1).

Now, we want to find out if there is an approximation algorithm for 2-HWP that has an approximation factor less than 3. Theorem 3.1 conclusively confirms the possibility. The proposed algorithm uses two subroutines. One is modified Christofide’s heuristic [11] to find the minimum-weight Hamiltonian path in a complete weighted graph. The other is an approximation algorithm for the maximum weighted rr-set packing problem (m​a​xr​S​P​Pmax_{r}SPP) [18], where we are given a collection of weighted sets, each of which contains at most rr elements from a fixed universe of finite elements. The goal is to find a sub-collection of pairwise disjoint sets with the maximum total weight.

Overview of the Improved Algorithm for 2-HWP: First, we create a weighted set-packing instance from the given unweighted graph GG (Section 3.1). Then, we apply an approximation algorithm of the set-packing problem to get a solution, and from that solution, we construct a tree T​r​(G)Tr(G) that spans all the vertices of VV (Section 3.2). Next, we find an open Hamiltonian walk in the tree T​r​(G)Tr(G), which gives us the required solution (Section 3.3). The proofs of all lemmas are excluded due to page limits.

3.1 Creating a set-packing instance from GG

From a given instance of 22-HWP, we first create an instance of m​a​x6​S​P​Pmax_{6}SPP, denoted as ℐS​P​(G)\mathcal{I}_{SP}(G). The motivation behind the construction is to select all possible cases from which we can get a 2-transition edge. These transitions may arise from a cycle of length four (C4)(C_{4}) or a grid of size 2×32\times 3 or any combination of the two. Finding such a disjoint collection of sets is preferable, as it reduces repeated visits to certain vertices. This can be achieved by applying the set-packing algorithm. However, it is possible that two C4C_{4}’s intersect at a single vertex (as shown in Fig. 4). In such cases, all vertices of two C4C_{4}’s can be traversed using 4 configurations. So, selecting only disjoint sets does not fully satisfy our objective. We define several types of packing sets to adapt such subgraphs in our solution.

We construct four types of weighted sets: two corresponding to each 4-length cycle C={v1,v2,v3,v4}C=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4}\}, and two corresponding to each 2×32\times 3 grid D={v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6}D=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4},v_{5},v_{6}\} in GG. Note that GG may not contain any C4C_{4}. In that case, we have a simpler algorithm with a better approximation factor, which is discussed at the end of the section (Theorem 2.2). However, our main focus is the arbitrary case where the graph may be dense and contains many C4C_{4}’s.

  • •

    (Type-I) A set C11=CC_{1}^{1}=C with weight four.

  • •

    (Type-II) Four sets, each of the form C2i=C∖{vi}∪{uCi}C_{2}^{i}=C\setminus\{{v_{i}}\}\cup\{{u_{C}^{i}}\} with weight three for 1≤i≤41\leq i\leq 4, where uCiu_{C}^{i} is a dummy variable corresponding to viv_{i}, not belonging to VV and not previously used in the construction process.

  • •

    (Type-III) A set D={v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6}D=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4},v_{5},v_{6}\} with weight six.

  • •

    (Type-IV) For each set DD of Type-III, we create another six sets, each of the form D∖{vi}∪{wDi}D\setminus\{{v_{i}}\}\cup\{{w_{D}^{i}}\} with weight five for 1≤i≤61\leq i\leq 6, where wDiw_{D}^{i} is a dummy variable corresponding to viv_{i}, not belonging to VV and not previously used.

We call all these sets the packing set. The weights are assigned according to how many vertices a packing set contains from the vertex set VV. Note that {v1,v2,v3,v4}\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4}\} being a cycle of length four, between the configurations (v1,v2)(v_{1},v_{2}) and (v4,v3)(v_{4},v_{3}), there is a transition edge. Similarly, if {v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6}\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4},v_{5},v_{6}\} is a grid of size 2×32\times 3, there must be two transition edges between (v1,v2)(v_{1},v_{2}) and (v4,v3)(v_{4},v_{3}), and between the configurations (v4,v3)(v_{4},v_{3}) and (v5,v6)(v_{5},v_{6}).

GG can have at most (n4)\binom{n}{4} cycles of length four. For each such cycle, we create one Type-I packing set and four Type-II packing sets. Furthermore, GG has at most (n6)\binom{n}{6} grids of size 2×32\times 3. For each such grid, we make one Type-III packing set and six Type-IV packing sets. Thus, for a given graph GG, we create at most 5⋅(n4)+7⋅(n6)=O⁡(n6)5\cdot\binom{n}{4}+7\cdot\binom{n}{6}=O(n^{6}) sets, where each set is of size at most six and the universal set of the procedure is V∪(∪C∈G∪i=14uCi)∪(∪D∈G∪j=16wDj)V\cup(\cup_{C\in G}\cup_{i=1}^{4}u_{C}^{i})\cup(\cup_{D\in G}\cup_{j=1}^{6}w_{D}^{j}), where CC is a 4 length cycle and DD is a 2×32\times 3 grid in GG. All uCiu_{C}^{i} and wDjw_{D}^{j} (OPEN∀i,j)\forall i,j) are distinct.

m​a​xk​S​P​Pmax_{k}SPP is NP-hard and since the introduction of the set packing problem, a significant research has been conducted in the past few decades for the weighted, unweighted, and online cases [1], [3], [8], [17], [18]. The best known polynomial-time approximation algorithm of the weighted kk-set packing problem is given by Thiery and Ward [18], achieving a factor slightly less than 2k+1\frac{2}{k+1}, which asymptotically approaches 42​k+1\frac{4}{2k+1} as kk grows. We define m​a​x6​(ℐ)max_{6}(\mathcal{I}) to represent the problem m​a​x6​S​P​Pmax_{6}SPP for the instance ℐ\mathcal{I}. We denote the optimal value of m​a​x6​(ℐS​P​(G))max_{6}(\mathcal{I}_{SP}(G)) by w⁡(O​P​TS​P​(G))w(OPT_{SP}(G)). Then the following lemma holds:

Lemma 8

h2​(G)≥(n−w⁡(O​P​TS​P​(G))2−1)h_{2}(G)\geq(n-\frac{w(OPT_{SP}(G))}{2}-1).

Our first step in designing an approximation algorithm is to create a tree T​r​(G)Tr(G) based on the approximate solution of m​a​x6​(ℐS​P​(G))max_{6}(\mathcal{I}_{SP}(G)). There are two types of vertices in the tree T​r​(G)Tr(G): some are the vertices of GG, and the remaining ones are the edges of GG, which we refer to as contracted vertices. We discuss the construction process in the following section.

3.3 Finding an open Hamiltonian walk on the tree T​r​(G)Tr(G)

The above procedure implies that an open Hamiltonian walk of T​r​(G)Tr(G) with one agent corresponds to an open walk of configurations with two agents that spans all the vertices in VV. Theorem 2.1 guarantees that for a tree with diameter dd and (n−1)(n-1) edges, the length of the optimal open Hamiltonian walk is 2​(n−1)−d2(n-1)-d. To find a better approximation result, here we give an alternative way to find the open Hamiltonian walk of T​r​(G)Tr(G) by using modified Christofide’s heuristic proposed by Hoogeveen [11]. The heuristic applies to the complete weighted graph with weight function satisfying the triangular inequality. Therefore, we first convert our constructed tree T​r​(G)Tr(G) into a complete weighted graph T​r∗​(G)Tr^{*}(G) as follows: each existing edge of T​r​(G)Tr(G) is assigned a weight of one, while each missing edge between two vertices t​r1tr_{1} and t​r2tr_{2} is given a weight equal to the length of the shortest path between them in the line graph of GG or in G, depending on whether the vertex is contracted or not. If t​r1tr_{1} or t​r2tr_{2} is a non-contracted vertex (i.e., in VV), we compute the length between them in GG. However, if both t​r1tr_{1} and t​r2tr_{2} are contracted vertices, we calculate the shortest length in the line graph of GG. By assigning weights this way, the triangular inequality is preserved. Next, similar to the modified Christofide’s heuristic, we first find the minimum spanning tree (M​S​TT​r∗MST_{Tr^{*}}) of the newly created graph T​r∗​(G)Tr^{*}(G), which gives the tree T​r​(G)Tr(G). Then we find the minimum matching (M​MT​r∗MM_{Tr^{*}}) between all the odd-degree vertices, except for two. The detail and analysis of this heuristic can be found in [11]. Let c​o​s​t​(M​S​TT​r∗)cost(MST_{Tr^{*}}) and c​o​s​t​(M​MT​r∗)cost(MM_{Tr^{*}}) be the cost of the M​S​TT​r∗MST_{Tr^{*}} and M​MT​r∗MM_{Tr^{*}}, respectively. We keep two odd-degree vertices unmatched as we look for the path, not the cycle. By adding the matching edges, all the vertices in T​r​(G)Tr(G) become even-degree vertices except two, which is sufficient to get an Eulerian path (a path traversing each edge exactly once). The length of this Eulerian path is c​o​s​t​(M​S​TT​r∗)+c​o​s​t​(M​MT​r∗)=l​e​n​(T​r​(G))+c​o​s​t​(M​MT​r∗)cost(MST_{Tr^{*}})+cost(MM_{Tr^{*}})=len(Tr(G))+cost(MM_{Tr^{*}}). This path can be easily modified to obtain an open walk of a configuration of GG with two agents, without changing its length. Hence, if the complete procedure as discussed above is referred to as A​L​G2ALG_{2}, then the length of the transition walk returned by A​L​G2ALG_{2} is tA​L​G2=l​e​n​(T​r​(G))+c​o​s​t​(M​MT​r∗)t_{ALG_{2}}=len(Tr(G))+cost(MM_{Tr^{*}}).

4 k-HWP on Hypergraphs

Here, we formulate the problem kk-HWP on hypergraphs and design an approximation algorithm to solve the problem. The formulation of the problem and the proposed solution will provide insight to obtain a solution for kk-HWP on the graph. A hypergraph generalizes a graph by allowing each hyperedge to connect any number of vertices. In this paper, we consider the undirected kk-uniform hypergraph without multiple edges, where each hyperedge connects exactly kk vertices. We misuse G=(V,E)G=(V,E) to represent both the graph and the hypergraph. However, a hyperedge in an kk-uniform hypergraph is a subset of VV of size kk. The line graph L⁡(G)L(G) of a hypergraph GG is a graph where each vertex represents a hyperedge of GG, and two vertices are adjacent if their corresponding hyperedges intersect. The hypergraph GG is connected if L⁡(G)L(G) is connected.

Before defining the problem on the hypergraph, let us revisit the problem formulation on the simple graph with k=2k=2. In 22-HWP, we traverse the graph via the edges, with transitions classified as shifts or jumps. If the transition edge between (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) and (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}) is a 1-transition edge, the pairs share a common vertex, and the move is called a “shift”. Otherwise, it’s a 2-transition edge, where one agent moves along (xi,xj)(x_{i},x_{j}) and the other along (yi,yj)(y_{i},y_{j}). After their movements, they reach (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}) and the transition is called “jump”. We introduce a similar notion for hypergraphs. Let all kk agents initially lie on kk distinct vertices {v10,v20,⋯,vk0}\{v_{1}^{0},v_{2}^{0},\cdots,v_{k}^{0}\} of GG such that there is a hyperedge of GG, say e0e_{0}, that connects all these vertices. In the next step, the movements are one of the following. (i) All agents move to a hyperedge e1∈Ee_{1}\in E such that e0e_{0} and e1e_{1} are adjacent, i.e., they share at least one vertex. This transition is named “shift”. (ii) ∀i:1≤i≤k\forall i:1\leq i\leq k the agent aia_{i} moves from vi0v_{i}^{0} to vi1v_{i}^{1} such that there exists a hyperedge that contains {vi0,vi1}\{v_{i}^{0},v_{i}^{1}\}. Moreover, there exists a hyperedge that contains all the vertices {v11,v21,⋯,vk1}\{v_{1}^{1},v_{2}^{1},\cdots,v_{k}^{1}\}. This transition is named “jump”. Thus, we can assume each configuration to be one of the hyperedges, and the traversal is through those hyperedges. We formally define the problem below. The NP-hardness of the problem is directly derived from the NP-hardness of 2-HWP, since the 2-uniform hypergraph is equivalent to a simple graph. An example of a hypergraph with its bipartite graph representation and one of the optimal solutions for kk-HWP on Hypergraph is depicted in Fig. 6

Definition 7 (Problem: kk-HWP on Hypergraph)

Consider an undirected connected kk-uniform hypergraph GG along with a collection of kk agents. The task is to find a sequence of configurations {𝒞i}\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\} with minimum length where each successive pair of configurations is adjacent, and every vertex in GG is included at least once in one of these configurations.

High-level Idea of the Approx. Algorithm for k-HWP on Hypergraph: We begin by computing the line graph L⁡(G)L(G) of the given hypergraph GG. The graph L⁡(G)L(G) contains only the shift edges. We then modify L⁡(G)L(G) by introducing all possible jump edges and denote the resulting graph by L∗​(G)L^{*}(G). Next, we search for a minimum length walk of L∗​(G)L^{*}(G) that spans all the vertices of VV. To achieve this, we create an instance ℐC​S​C​(G)\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G) of the minimum connected set cover problem (MCSC) [20] from the graph L∗​(G)L^{*}(G). In MCSC, we are given an universe of elements UU, a family of subsets ℱ={S}\mathcal{F}=\{S\} where each S⊆US\subseteq U, and a connected graph where each vertex represents a unique S∈ℱS\in\mathcal{F}. The objective is to find a minimum size subfamily ℱ′⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F} such that each element of UU is present in some of the members of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and the vertices associated with ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} induce a connected subgraph of the given graph. For ℐC​S​C​(G)\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G), we consider the vertex set VV as the universe, the set of hyperedges EE as the family of subsets, and L∗​(G)L^{*}(G) is the underlying connected subgraph. Using the best known approximation algorithm for MCSC by Zhang et al. [20], which is of factor (1+ln⁡k)(1+\ln k), we derive a connected subgraph of L∗​(G)L^{*}(G), say S​o​lSol, that covers all the vertices of VV. Finally, we transform S​o​lSol into a walk by doubling all its edges, yielding a solution of k-HWP on the hypergraph GG. The size of the solution is

Detailed Description of the Approximation Algorithm for k-HWP on Hypergraph: First, we compute the line graph L⁡(G)L(G) of the given hypergraph GG. The edges of L⁡(G)L(G) consist only of the shift edges. So, we remain to search all possible jump edges. Therefore, we determine the open neighbourhood N⁡(vi)N(v_{i}) of each vertex viv_{i}, which is the set of vertices uiu_{i} such that there exists an edge e′∈Ee^{\prime}\in E that contains {ui,vi}\{u_{i},v_{i}\}. Now, for each edge e={v1,v2,⋯,vk}∈Ee=\{v_{1},v_{2},\cdots,v_{k}\}\in E, we consider all possible sets of the form {u1,u2,⋯,uk}\{u_{1},u_{2},\cdots,u_{k}\}, where ui∈N⁡(vi)​∀i∈{1,2,⋯,k}u_{i}\in N(v_{i})~\forall i\in\{1,2,\cdots,k\}, and check if there is an edge e′′e^{\prime\prime} that connects the vertices {u1,u2,⋯,uk}\{u_{1},u_{2},\cdots,u_{k}\}. If so, add an edge between ee and e′′e^{\prime\prime} on the line graph L⁡(G)L(G). There are at most k⋅Δ⁡(G)k\cdot\Delta(G) such sets for each e∈Ee\in E, where Δ⁡(G)=maxv∈V⁡|N⁡(v)|\Delta(G)=\max_{v\in V}|N(v)|. We can discover all the jump edges in polynomial time. Let us give an unique id to each vertex vi∈Vv_{i}\in V from the set {1,2,⋯,n}\{1,2,\cdots,n\}. We assume that the kk-uniform hypergraph is stored in a kk-dimensional array. The entry of (i1,i2,⋯,ik}⊂{1,2,⋯,n}(i_{1},i_{2},\cdots,i_{k}\}\subset\{1,2,\cdots,n\} is one if there is an edge that connects the vertices {v1,v2,⋯,vk}\{v_{1},v_{2},\cdots,v_{k}\}, otherwise zero. So, we can find whether there is an edge that connects the vertices {u1,u2,⋯,uk}\{u_{1},u_{2},\cdots,u_{k}\} in O⁡(k)O(k) time. Thus, for a fixed hyperedge ee, we can find all edges e′′e^{\prime\prime} for which there is a jump edge between them in O⁡(k2⋅Δ⁡(G))O(k^{2}\cdot\Delta(G)) time. Hence, all the jump edges of the line graph L⁡(G)L(G) can be computed in O⁡(m⋅k2⋅Δ⁡(G))O(m\cdot k^{2}\cdot\Delta(G)), where mm is the number of hyperedges of GG. We denote this modified line graph by L∗​(G)L^{*}(G). Any solution of kk-HWP on hypergraphs is an open walk on graph L∗​(G)L^{*}(G). Thus, the problem reduces to finding a minimum length walk of the graph L∗​(G)L^{*}(G) that covers all the vertices of VV. We solve it using a subroutine of the minimum connected set cover problem, defined below.

Minimum Connected Set Cover Problem(MCSC): We have given a universe UU of elements and a family ℱ={S}\mathcal{F}=\{S\} of subsets of that universe such that ∪SS∈ℱ=V\cup S_{S\in\mathcal{F}}=V. Any set cover is a subfamily ℱ′⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F} such that each element of UU is present in one of the elements in ℱ′\mathcal{F^{\prime}}. Minimum set cover is the set cover with the minimum cardinality. The instance of the MCSC contains an additional connected graph whose vertex set is ℱ\mathcal{F}, which means that each S∈ℱS\in\mathcal{F} is considered a vertex of the graph. The objective is to find a set cover ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} with minimum cardinality such that the vertices associated with ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} induce a connected subgraph of the given graph. Finding a minimum set cover is NP-hard. A simple greedy algorithm gives an approximation factor (1+ln⁡(Δ))(1+\ln(\Delta)), which is calculated using the pricing method and Δ=maxS∈ℱ⁡|S|\Delta=\max_{S\in\mathcal{F}}|S|. Trevisan [19] showed that the problem cannot be approximated within the factor (ln⁡(Δ)−O⁡(ln⁡(ln⁡(Δ))))(\ln(\Delta)-O(\ln(\ln(\Delta)))) unless P=NP. Dinur and Steurer [7] also established that the approximation of the set cover problem to within factor (1−ϵ)​ln⁡n(1-\epsilon)\ln n is NP hard for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and nn being the size of the universe. This result ensures that the (1+ln⁡(Δ))(1+\ln(\Delta))-approximation algorithm is asymptotically best unless P=NP. Zhang et al. [20] proposed the (1+ln⁡(Δ))(1+\ln(\Delta))-approximation algorithm and an inapproximable bound to the MCSC.

From a given instance of kk-HWP in hypergraph (GG), we can construct an instance ℐC​S​C​(G)\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G) of the connected set cover problem by considering the vertex set (V)(V) as the universe, the set of hyperedges (EE) as the family of subsets, and the line graph L∗​(G)L^{*}(G) as the underlying connected subgraph. Any solution to kk-HWP on hypergraph GG is a feasible solution to the connected set cover problem for the instance ℐC​S​C​(G)\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G). So O​P​T​(ℐC​S​C​(G))≤hk​(G)OPT(\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G))\leq h_{k}(G), where O​P​T​(ℐC​S​C​(G))OPT(\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G)) is the optimum solution to the connected set cover problem for the instance ℐC​S​C​(G)\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G). Let S​o​lSol be a solution to the connected set cover problem for the instance ℐC​S​C​(G)\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G) using a β\beta-approximation algorithm from the literature, and let |S​o​l||Sol| be the size of that solution. Then |S​o​l|≤β⋅O​P​T​(ℐC​S​C​(G))|Sol|\leq\beta\cdot OPT(\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G)). For a given connected subgraph of L∗​(G)L^{*}(G) induced by the vertices of S​o​lSol, we can always construct a walk, by doubling all the edges and then finding an Eulerian walk. This walk is of length at most 2​|S​o​l|2|Sol|, which forms a feasible solution to kk-HWP on the hypergraph GG. So we have an approximate solution (A​L​GH​G)(ALG_{HG}) to kk-HWP on GG with a solution size (tA​L​GH​G)(t_{ALG_{HG}}) at most 2⋅|S​o​l|≤2⋅β⋅O​P​T​(ℐC​S​C​(G))≤2​β⋅hk​(G)2\cdot|Sol|\leq 2\cdot\beta\cdot OPT(\mathcal{I}_{CSC}(G))\leq 2\beta\cdot h_{k}(G).

Theorem 4.1

There exists a 2​(1+ln⁡k)2(1+\ln k)-approximation algorithm for kk-HWP on hypergraph.

Proof

We obtain the factor by applying the best known approximation algorithm of the connected set cover problem, which is proposed by Zhang et al. [20], i.e., by setting β=(1+ln⁡k)\beta=(1+\ln k), as in our case Δ=k\Delta=k. ∎

Theorem 4.2

There exists a 2​(1+ln⁡k)2(1+\ln k)-approximation algorithm for kk-HWP on a simple graph, when k=O⁡(1)k=O(1).

Proof

For a given connected graph GG, we construct an instance of the connected set cover problem, where the universe is the vertex set VV, and the family of subsets (ℱ)(\mathcal{F}) consists of all possible connected subgraphs of GG of size kk. There can be at most nkn^{k} such subsets of VV. For a given S⊂VS\subset V of size kk, we check the connectivity of the induced subgraph made by the vertices of SS in O⁡(k+m)O(k+m) time. Therefore, we need nO⁡(k)n^{O(k)} time to construct the family ℱ\mathcal{F}. Next, we build the underlying connected graph GG in a manner similar to the above process mentioned in the algorithm for k-HWP on hypergraph. The only difference is that, for each vertex vi∈Vv_{i}\in V we consider its closed neighbourhood N⁡[vi]=N⁡(vi)∪{vi}N[v_{i}]=N(v_{i})\cup\{v_{i}\}, as in the definition of kk-HWP on the graph allows an agent to remain stationary. Thus, by a similar argument to that above, we can estimate the proposed result. However, the complexity of time is dominated by the polynomial nkn^{k}. So, the algorithm runs in polynomial-time algorithm only if k=O⁡(1)k=O(1). ∎

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we examine the Hamiltonian walk problem within the context of a connected group of mobile agents that minimally traverse the graph. The NP-hardness of the problem leads us to find some approximation algorithms. We propose an approximation algorithm for the problem with a set of two agents for any arbitrary graph. Then we define the problem on hypergraphs and provide an approximation algorithm. We also show some optimal results for the acyclic graph. Additionally, we define a restricted version of the problem in which each transition explores only one new vertex compared to the previous one. In the future, exploring tighter bounds for the problem and investigating the class of graphs in which a polynomial solution exists will be interesting.
